content: Tinospora cordifolia, commonly referred to as Guduchi, is a herbaceous vine belonging to the Menispermaceae family. It is native to tropical regions of India, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka. The plant is a climbing shrub that thrives in these tropical climates. The stems of Tinospora cordifolia are typically harvested during the hot season and subsequently dried for medicinal use. The dried stems are found in either straight or twisted cylindrical forms, as well as in slices. These pieces generally measure about 2 centimeters in diameter, although smaller fragments are also common. Externally, the stems are covered with a thin, papery, brown cork layer, which is marked by raised scars from numerous lenticels. This cork layer can be easily exfoliated, revealing a greenish cortex beneath. The cortex is longitudinally wrinkled and also marked with lenticels. When broken, the stem exhibits a fibrous fracture. A transverse section of the stem reveals a yellowish wood with radially arranged, wedge-shaped wood bundles. These bundles contain large vessels and are separated by narrower medullary rays. The plant has no distinctive odor, but its taste is notably bitter. The active constituents of Tinospora cordifolia include a variety of diterpene compounds such as tinosporone, tinosporic acid, and cordifolisides A to E. Other notable components include syringen, the yellow alkaloid berberine, giloin, crude giloinin, and a glucosidal bitter principle. Additionally, the plant contains polysaccharides, including arabinogalactan polysaccharide (TSP), which contribute to its adaptogenic properties. Ethnobotanically, Tinospora cordifolia has been used in traditional Indian medicine for centuries. It has been employed in the preparation of a starch known as giloe-ka-sat or palo. The plant is reputed to possess tonic, antiperiodic, and diuretic properties. Historical pharmacological studies, such as those by Flückiger, identified traces of an alkaloid and a bitter glucoside in the plant. The British Pharmacopoeia of 1900 recognized its medicinal value and included preparations such as an infusion (Infusum Tinosporae) and a tincture (Tinctura Tinosporae). The recommended dosage for the infusion was 15 to 30 milliliters (one-half to one fluid ounce).
